provenance.snapshot_text: H.264, officially titled Advanced video coding for generic audiovisual services, is the ITU-T recommendation for compressing digital video.
H.264 divides each video frame into macroblocks of 16x16 luma samples, which can be split into smaller partitions as small as 4x4 for motion-compensated prediction.

I-frames are self-contained and do not require other frames to decode; P-frames and B-frames reduce file size by referencing already-decoded frames, with B-frames referencing frames from both before and after.

It processes each frame in fixed 16x16 macroblocks that can be split into smaller partitions for motion-compensated prediction, and it classifies frames as self-contained I-frames or as P-frames/B-frames that reduce size by referencing already-decoded frames.

claims.statement: H.264 is the ITU-T/ISO standard, titled Advanced Video Coding, for compressing digital video.
H.264 divides each video frame into 16x16-pixel macroblocks, splittable into smaller partitions for motion-compensated prediction.
H.264 frames are I-frames, P-frames, or B-frames: I-frames stand alone, while P-frames and B-frames shrink file size by referencing already-decoded frames.

sections.text: H.264, also known as Advanced Video Coding, is the ITU-T and ISO standard most video you watch today is compressed with. Its job is to shrink raw video down to a fraction of its size while keeping it watchable, so it can be streamed and stored practically.

To compress a single frame, H.264 splits it into fixed 16 by 16 pixel blocks called macroblocks. Each macroblock can be broken down further, into partitions as small as 4 by 4 pixels, so the encoder can track motion and detail at whatever scale actually changed.

Across frames, H.264 uses three frame types. I-frames stand alone, like a single photograph. P-frames and B-frames instead store only what changed relative to other frames, with B-frames referencing both earlier and later frames, which is why most of a video's data comes from just a few I-frames.
